name: Dhruv Batra
bio:
Dhruv Batra is a co-founder and the Chief Scientist of Yutori, building web agents.  

Before this, he was a Senior Director at Meta leading FAIR Embodied AI, and an Associate Professor at Georgia Tech. 

He received the 2019 Presidential early career award for scientists and engineers (PECASE) from the White House for his work on explainable AI and neural network interpretability. 
He and his collaborators received the 2025 Mark Everingham Prize for their 2015 work on Visual Question Answering that established "a new strand of vision and language research.”
He is a recipient of best paper awards/nominations in every area of AI (vision, NLP, ML, robotics).

positions.claim: The web will be agentified by computer-use models operating on pixels, not by websites exposing APIs.
Popular head-of-distribution websites may provide APIs, but the long tail will not.
For structured, aggregator-backed tasks like flight search, using a computer-use agent to click buttons is the wrong design — you should call the existing API.
There are roughly 200 million active websites and close to a billion total, and their infrastructure changes very slowly.
Coding agents pointed at raw HTML cannot reliably extract page content, because content is fetched asynchronously and computed by rendering logic rather than present as text.
Writing per-site scaffolds is a losing strategy because it fails to generalize to the long tail; the general screenshot-in solution wins.
Computer-use agents should not be restricted to human-like interaction; they should write and execute code when useful while verifying outcomes through pixels.
The perception that progress on computer use has been slow is wrong and is not supported by benchmark numbers.
Mind2Web is saturated at 97% human eval and should be retired in favor of a harder benchmark.
Yutori's accuracy edge over Opus 4.7 and GPT-5.5 is within statistical noise; the real advantage is latency per step and cost per task.
Smaller-footprint computer-use models are substantially faster than trillion-plus parameter frontier models on browser tasks.
The claim that computer-use agents are slow and expensive is largely true today but is being optimized away.
AI agents becoming the primary drivers of action on the web is essentially uncontestable.
Thirty years of human-oriented web infrastructure will not be reinvented for machines within 2-10 years.
Once computer-use agents are sub-penny, sub-100ms, and return structured output, the distinction between them and an API stops mattering.
Multi-agent orchestration of parallel browser sandboxes enables superhuman throughput no individual human could match.
